documents.title: Deep Neural Networks Learn Meta-Structures to Segment Fluorescence Microscopy Images

texts.raid-human: Fluorescence microscopy images play the critical role of capturing spatial or spatiotemporal information of biomedical processes in life sciences. Their simple structures and semantics provide unique advantages in elucidating learning behavior of deep neural networks (DNNs). It is generally assumed that accurate image annotation is required to train DNNs for accurate image segmentation. In this study, however, we find that DNNs trained by label images in which nearly half (49%) of the binary pixel labels are randomly flipped provide largely the same segmentation performance. This suggests that DNNs learn high-level structures rather than pixel-level labels per se to segment fluorescence microscopy images. We refer to these structures as meta-structures. In support of the existence of the meta-structures, when DNNs are trained by a series of label images with progressively less meta-structure information, we find progressive degradation in their segmentation performance. Motivated by the learning behavior of DNNs trained by random labels and the characteristics of meta-structures, we propose an unsupervised segmentation model. Experiments show that it achieves remarkably competitive performance in comparison to supervised segmentation models.
texts.raid-chatgpt: This paper presents a novel approach for segmenting fluorescence microscopy images using deep neural networks. The authors propose a method that leverages the ability of deep neural networks to learn meta-structures, which are higher-level structures that capture the relationships between different objects in the image. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on a benchmark dataset and demonstrates the effectiveness of using meta-structures for image segmentation tasks. The results suggest that deep neural networks can learn to extract meaningful information from fluorescence microscopy images and improve the accuracy of segmentation algorithms. This research has implications for the field of biomedical imaging and can potentially contribute to advancements in automated image analysis and understanding.
texts.raid-gpt4: This paper presents a novel approach to segment fluorescence microscopy images using deep neural networks (DNNs). The study demonstrates that DNNs can learn meta-structures, which are complex patterns that cannot be easily identified by traditional image processing techniques. The proposed method involves training DNNs on a large dataset of fluorescence microscopy images, allowing the networks to automatically learn the underlying meta-structures. The results show that the DNNs can accurately segment the images, outperforming existing methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. This research opens up new possibilities for automated image analysis in biological research and medical diagnostics.
texts.raid-llama-chat:
In this paper, we present a novel approach for segmenting fluorescence microscopy images using deep neural networks. Our approach leverages the concept of meta-structures, which are high-level abstractions of the underlying image structure that can be learned from a set of training images. By incorporating meta-structures into the network architecture, we enable the network to learn a hierarchical representation of the image data that can be used for accurate segmentation.

We evaluate our approach on several datasets of fluorescence microscopy images and demonstrate its superior performance compared to traditional segmentation methods. Our experiments show that the use of meta-structures improves the accuracy and efficiency of the segmentation process, and enables the network to generalize well to new images.

The main contributions of this paper are:

* The introduction of meta-structures as a new concept for segmenting fluorescence microscopy images using deep neural networks.
* The development of a novel network architecture that incorporates meta-structures to learn a hierarchical representation of the image data.
* The evaluation of our approach on several datasets, demonstrating its superior performance and generalization ability compared to traditional segmentation methods.

Our work has important implications for the analysis of fluorescence microscopy images, which is a critical tool in many biological and biomedical applications. The proposed method can help to automate the segmentation process, reduce the amount of manual effort required, and improve the accuracy and consistency of the results.

documents.title: A Generalized Asymmetric Dual-front Model for Active Contours and Image Segmentation

In this paper, we introduce a type of asymmetric quadratic metrics dual-front model. The metrics considered are built by the integration of the image features and a vector field derived from the evolving contours. The use of the asymmetry enhancement can reduce the risk of contour shortcut or leakage problems especially when the initial contours are far away from the target boundaries or the images have complicated intensity distributions. Moreover, the proposed dual-front model can be applied for image segmentation in conjunction with various region-based homogeneity terms. The numerical experiments on both synthetic and real images show that the proposed dual-front model indeed achieves encouraging results.

documents.title: A Thorough View of Exact Inference in Graphs from the Degree-4 Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy

texts.raid-human: Performing inference in graphs is a common task within several machine learning problems, e.g., image segmentation, community detection, among others. For a given undirected connected graph, we tackle the statistical problem of exactly recovering an unknown ground-truth binary labeling of the nodes from a single corrupted observation of each edge. Such problem can be formulated as a quadratic combinatorial optimization problem over the boolean hypercube, where it has been shown before that one can (with high probability and in polynomial time) exactly recover the ground-truth labeling of graphs that have an isoperimetric number that grows with respect to the number of nodes (e.g., complete graphs, regular expanders). In this work, we apply a powerful hierarchy of relaxations, known as the sum-of-squares (SoS) hierarchy, to the combinatorial problem. Motivated by empirical evidence on the improvement in exact recoverability, we center our attention on the degree-4 SoS relaxation and set out to understand the origin of such improvement from a graph theoretical perspective. We show that the solution of the dual of the relaxed problem is related to finding edge weights of the Johnson and Kneser graphs, where the weights fulfill the SoS constraints and intuitively allow the input graph to increase its algebraic connectivity. Finally, as byproduct of our analysis, we derive a novel Cheeger-type lower bound for the algebraic connectivity of graphs with signed edge weights.

texts.raid-claude: Performing exact inference in graphs is a recurring task in machine learning, arising in problems such as image segmentation, community detection, and correlation clustering. Given an undirected connected graph and a single noisy observation of each edge, the goal is to exactly recover an unknown ground-truth binary labeling of the nodes. This problem can be cast as a quadratic combinatorial optimization over the Boolean hypercube, which is NP-hard in general, and is therefore commonly attacked by convex relaxations. The degree-2 relaxation from the sum-of-squares hierarchy, i.e., the standard semidefinite program, has been studied extensively and its exact recovery behavior is well characterized in terms of a spectral quantity of the graph. The degree-4 relaxation is provably tighter and succeeds in regimes where the degree-2 relaxation fails, but it is generally dismissed as computationally prohibitive, since it optimizes over a matrix whose dimension grows quadratically with the number of nodes. In this work we give a thorough view of the degree-4 case. We exploit the structure of the moment matrix to obtain a low-rank, Burer-Monteiro-style parameterization, and we analyze a projected gradient method over this non-convex landscape, establishing a per-iteration cost and a linear convergence rate to a solution from which the ground truth is read off. On the statistical side, we derive sufficient conditions for exact recovery that depend on the connectivity of the graph and on the noise level, and we show analytically that these conditions are weaker than the best known conditions for the degree-2 relaxation, quantifying the gain of moving one level up the hierarchy. We also clarify when the extra level does not help, characterizing graph families for which the two relaxations share the same recovery threshold. Experiments on synthetic graphs corroborate our theory and illustrate the predicted separation between the two levels of the hierarchy.

We propose an attention-based encoder-decoder architecture in which residual attention modules and channel-spatial attention gates suppress responses from stratigraphic reflectors and acquisition noise while amplifying thin, laterally discontinuous fault signatures, addressing the severe foreground-background imbalance that characterizes fault labels. To exploit incomplete supervision, we introduce a masked loss formulation that back-propagates only through labeled slices, combined with a binary cross-entropy and Dice objective, so that unlabeled voxels contribute no spurious negative gradients.
